name: Paris — the city above and below
scope: The French capital on the Seine, built in layers above and below ground. T1: beneath the streets lie the CATACOMBS — former limestone quarries where the neatly stacked bones of about SIX MILLION Parisians were moved in the 1780s when the old cemeteries overflowed. T2: the quarries came first — Paris was largely built from Lutetian limestone dug out from UNDER itself, leaving a honeycomb of tunnels that later swallowed the dead. T3: on the Île de la Cité, the SAINTE-CHAPELLE is a glass cage — 15 towering windows holding 1,113 scenes, built in the 1240s by King Louis IX to house the Crown of Thorns relic. T4: at street level, Hector Guimard's swirling green cast-iron MÉTRO entrances (c. 1900) are the icons of ART NOUVEAU, the 'new art' style, born in that moment. T5: the EIFFEL TOWER, 300 m of wrought iron built for the 1889 fair, is a living thermometer — iron expands in summer heat, so the tower grows about 15 cm taller and tilts slightly away from the sun. (Optional rung: PÈRE LACHAISE, opened 1804, the world's most-visited cemetery — Chopin, Wilde, Piaf, Morrison.)
source: Grokipedia (Catacombs of Paris; Sainte-Chapelle; Eiffel Tower) checked first at build; corroborated: Wikipedia (Catacombs of Paris; Sainte-Chapelle; Paris Métro entrances / Hector Guimard; Eiffel Tower thermal expansion); sainte-chapelle.fr (15 windows / 1,113 scenes); history.com (Catacombs origins).
framing_note: PLACE = Paris; every answer is a concrete Paris wonder (the Catacombs, the Sainte-Chapelle glass, the Métro's Art Nouveau railings, the growing iron tower). Scene-led — open on the six-million-bones tunnels or the 1,113 glowing panes, never 'What is the capital of France?'. Accuracy rail: the Catacombs hold remains MOVED from overflowing cemeteries (not people who died there), and '~6 million' is an estimate. Dinner-test payoff = the Eiffel Tower growing ~15 cm in summer heat (thermal expansion). Distractors stay live with other real Paris sites (Notre-Dame, the Louvre, the Panthéon). Lane border: keep answers to the PLACE, not French cuisine (cooking bank).

name: London — the city on the tidal Thames
scope: England's capital on the tidal River Thames, a city that keeps reinventing what lies under it. T1: at least six RAVENS are kept at the TOWER OF LONDON because legend says if the ravens ever leave, the Tower will crumble and the kingdom fall — so their wing feathers are trimmed. T2: the LONDON UNDERGROUND, opened in 1863 as the Metropolitan Railway, was the WORLD'S FIRST underground railway — steam trains running through gas-lit brick tunnels, ~38,000 riders on day one. T3: the GREAT FIRE OF 1666 began in a Pudding Lane bakery and burned for days, destroying about 13,000 houses and old St Paul's, yet the recorded death toll was tiny. T4: the fire let Christopher Wren rebuild ST PAUL'S CATHEDRAL with its great dome, whose 'Whispering Gallery' carries a whisper right around the dome's inner wall. T5: because London sits on a tidal river that funnels North Sea surges upstream, the THAMES BARRIER (built 1982) — steel gates that rotate up from the riverbed — is raised to hold back the sea. (Optional rung: the ROMAN wall of Londinium still shows in the City; London began as a Roman port around AD 47.)
source: Grokipedia (Tower of London; London Underground; Great Fire of London; Thames Barrier) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Tower of London ravens; History of the London Underground / Metropolitan Railway; Great Fire of London; St Paul's Cathedral; Thames Barrier); London Transport Museum ('World's first Underground').
framing_note: PLACE = London; answers are concrete London wonders (the raven legend, the first Underground, the Great Fire, the whispering dome, the Thames Barrier). Invert the wonder — '38,000 rode it on day one' → the world's first subway; 'it burned 13,000 houses but killed almost no one' → the Great Fire of 1666. Accuracy rail: the raven legend is LEGEND (say so); the load-bearing fact is '1863 = world's first underground railway'. Dinner-test payoff = the six ravens whose departure supposedly topples the kingdom. Lane border: keep to the PLACE, not Stuart or Tudor politics (history bank).
history_overlap: Great Fire of 1666 rung may touch a history-bank London episode; keep the geography answer the fire/place, not Restoration politics.

name: Rome — the Eternal City's engineering
scope: The Eternal City on the Tiber, built on seven hills and on 2,000-year-old engineering. T1: the PANTHEON's dome has a round hole — the OCULUS, about 9 m across — open to the sky at its top; rain falls straight through onto a slightly domed, drained floor. T2: that dome, 43.3 m across, is still the world's LARGEST UNREINFORCED CONCRETE DOME after ~1,900 years — the Romans lightened it upward, using heavy stone at the base and light pumice near the top. T3: Roman concrete outlasts modern concrete because it is SELF-HEALING — 'hot-mixed' lime leaves tiny lime clasts that dissolve and re-crystallize to fill cracks (confirmed by MIT in 2023); the key ingredient, pozzolana volcanic ash, came from Pozzuoli near Naples. T4: the APPIAN WAY (Via Appia), begun in 312 BC by Appius Claudius Caecus, was the 'queen of roads' — a stone-paved highway you can still walk today. T5: eleven AQUEDUCTS, starting with the Aqua Appia (312 BC), carried water into Rome by GRAVITY alone, dropping only a few centimetres per kilometre across miles of arches and tunnels. (Optional rungs: the COLOSSEUM's ~50,000 seats and its retractable awning; the CLOACA MAXIMA, one of the world's oldest sewers, still draining into the Tiber.)
source: Grokipedia (Pantheon, Rome; Roman concrete; Appian Way; Roman aqueducts) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Pantheon, Rome; Roman concrete; Appian Way; Roman aqueducts; Cloaca Maxima); MIT News 2023 (self-healing Roman concrete / lime clasts); ScienceAlert (pozzolana from Pozzuoli).
framing_note: PLACE = Rome; answers are concrete Roman marvels (the open oculus, the unreinforced dome, self-healing concrete, the Appian Way, gravity aqueducts). Teach a term before testing it (oculus, aqueduct, unreinforced). Accuracy rail: the self-healing / lime-clast mechanism is the 2023 MIT finding — state it as the current best explanation, and note pozzolana ash came from near Naples (a deliberate cross-link to the Naples ladder). Dinner-test payoff = rain falling through the Pantheon's open oculus onto a drained floor. Distractors = other real Roman sites (Colosseum, Forum, Circus Maximus). Lane border: engineering/place, not emperors' biographies (history bank).

name: Florence — Brunelleschi's impossible dome
scope: The Tuscan city on the Arno where the Renaissance was born, crowned by an engineering miracle. T1: Florence's cathedral, Santa Maria del Fiore, is topped by BRUNELLESCHI'S DOME — the largest brick-and-masonry dome ever raised, finished in 1436. T2: the astonishing part is HOW it stands: it was built WITHOUT a wooden support frame ('centering') underneath — no forest could have propped a dome that wide — so it had to hold ITSELF up as it rose. T3: Brunelleschi laid the bricks in a HERRINGBONE (spina-pesce) pattern that locked each ring in place and passed the weight to the ribs, letting the masons build a self-supporting spiral. T4: it is actually a DOUBLE dome — an inner shell and an outer shell with a staircase climbing between them — which made it lighter and let visitors walk up inside the wall. T5: nobody fully knew Brunelleschi's method — he left almost no plans and reportedly won the commission by challenging rivals to stand an egg on end, then cracking its base flat. (Optional rung: the PONTE VECCHIO, the old shop-lined bridge, was the only Florence bridge the retreating Germans did NOT blow up in 1944.)
source: Grokipedia (Florence Cathedral; Filippo Brunelleschi) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Florence Cathedral; Ponte Vecchio); duomo.firenze.it (self-supporting dome, no centering, herringbone brick, double shell).
framing_note: PLACE = Florence; answers are concrete facts about Brunelleschi's dome and the city (self-supporting, herringbone brick, double shell). Invert the wonder: 'the widest brick dome ever, and no wooden frame held it up while it was built' → it had to support itself as it rose. Accuracy rail: 'largest BRICK/masonry dome' (not largest dome of any kind — the Pantheon's is wider but concrete); the egg story is a REPORTED anecdote, flag it. Dinner-test payoff = a dome that held itself up with no scaffolding beneath it. Lane border: keep to architecture/place, not Medici politics (history) or Tuscan food (cooking).

name: Venice — the city on a sunken forest
scope: A city of 100+ islands built in a saltwater LAGOON, standing on a drowned forest. T1: Venice's stone palaces don't rest on rock — they stand on MILLIONS of wooden PILES driven down into the mud of the lagoon. T2: those submerged piles don't rot — starved of oxygen in the mud, the wood PETRIFIES, turning hard and stone-like over the centuries. T3: ACQUA ALTA ('high water') floods the city when high tides and south winds push the Adriatic into the lagoon; St Mark's Square, the lowest point, floods first — the great 1966 flood hit 194 cm. T4: to defend itself Venice built MOSE — 78 hollow steel gates lying flat on the seabed at the three lagoon inlets, that fill with air and swing up to seal out the sea (operational 2020). T5: on MURANO, a separate island, the Republic forced its glassmakers to move in 1291 — officially to keep their furnace fires from burning down wooden Venice, and to guard the secrets of Venetian glass. (Optional rung: Venice is slowly SINKING while the sea rises — the reason the barriers were built.)
source: Grokipedia (Venice; MOSE; Murano) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Venice; MOSE — 78 gates; Murano — 1291 glassmaker relocation; acqua alta records 1966=194 cm, 2019=187 cm).
framing_note: PLACE = Venice; answers are concrete lagoon-city wonders (wood piles, petrified wood, acqua alta, MOSE gates, the Murano fire-move). Invert the wonder: 'stone palaces on a mudflat — what holds them up?' → millions of wooden piles. Accuracy rail: the piles PETRIFY/harden in oxygen-poor mud (mineralized, not literally turned to rock — say 'petrified'); the 1291 Murano move was partly a fire-safety measure. Dinner-test payoff = a marble city standing on a sunken forest of petrified wood. Lane border: the PLACE and its water-engineering, not Venetian trade-empire politics (history) or cuisine (cooking).

name: Naples & the Bay of Fire
scope: Naples sits on the Bay of Naples between TWO volcanoes — one famous, one far more dangerous. T1: to the east looms VESUVIUS, whose eruption in AD 79 buried the Roman towns of POMPEII and Herculaneum, freezing a whole city in ash. T2: Vesuvius is still active (it last erupted in 1944) and about 3 million people now live within reach of it — one of the most densely populated danger zones on Earth. T3: to the WEST lies the bigger threat: the CAMPI FLEGREI ('burning fields'), a SUPERVOLCANO — not a cone but a huge sunken CALDERA about 12–15 km wide, with a whole town (Pozzuoli) built inside it. T4: the ground there breathes — BRADYSEISM ('slow earthquake') lifts and drops the land by metres over years as pressure shifts below; the columns of Pozzuoli's Roman market carry sea-mollusc borings high up, proof the ground sank underwater and later rose again. T5: beneath the city runs NAPLES UNDERGROUND — tunnels the Greeks began quarrying ~2,500 years ago for tuff building stone, reused as Roman aqueducts and later as WWII air-raid shelters, all cut into the same soft volcanic rock the volcanoes laid down.
source: Grokipedia (Mount Vesuvius; Campi Flegrei; Pompeii) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Mount Vesuvius; Pompeii; Campi Flegrei; bradyseism; Naples underground geothermal zone); Napoli Sotterranea (Greek quarry tunnels / WWII shelters); Macellum of Pozzuoli (mollusc borings on columns).
framing_note: PLACE = Naples and its bay; answers are concrete earth-science wonders of the place (Vesuvius / AD 79, the Campi Flegrei caldera, bradyseism, the tuff tunnels). Teach the terms (caldera, supervolcano, bradyseism) before testing them. Accuracy rail: the AD 79 and 1944 dates are firm; frame Campi Flegrei's danger as monitored scientific fact, not doom-mongering. Dinner-test payoff = the ground of Pozzuoli visibly rising and sinking (bradyseism), shown by sea-shell borings high on ancient columns. Lane border: the PLACE / earth-process, not Neapolitan pizza (cooking bank) — the pozzolana-ash link lives on the Rome-concrete ladder as a cross-reference.

name: Barcelona — Gaudí's growing basilica
scope: The Catalan capital on the Mediterranean, shaped by one visionary architect and one radical city plan. T1: the SAGRADA FAMÍLIA is Antoni Gaudí's great basilica — begun in 1882 and, famously, a building site for over 140 years. T2: in 2026 its central TOWER OF JESUS CHRIST was topped out at 172.5 m, making the Sagrada Família the TALLEST CHURCH in the world (passing Germany's Ulm Minster). T3: Gaudí deliberately made that tower ONE METRE lower than Barcelona's Montjuïc hill — he believed his work should not rise above God's. T4: Gaudí designed with NATURE and physics — tree-like branching columns and 'catenary' arches shaped like a hanging chain flipped upside-down, so the stone stands in pure compression. T5: across the city his buildings (Casa Batlló, Casa Milà) ripple like bone and water, while the EIXAMPLE grid around them — Ildefons Cerdà's 1859 plan — gives every block CHAMFERED (cut-off) corners to open up light and sightlines. (Gaudí is buried in the Sagrada Família's crypt.)
source: Grokipedia (Sagrada Família; Antoni Gaudí) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Sagrada Família; Antoni Gaudí; Eixample / Cerdà Plan); 2026 completion coverage (CNN, Vatican News, designboom — Tower of Jesus Christ 172.5 m, world's tallest church; Ulm Minster 161.5 m surpassed Oct 2025).
framing_note: PLACE = Barcelona; answers are concrete Gaudí/Barcelona facts (the still-growing basilica, the 172.5 m tower, the one-metre-below-Montjuïc rule, catenary/branching structure, the chamfered Eixample grid). Accuracy rail: as of 2026 the CENTRAL TOWER is complete and it IS now the world's tallest church — say the tower/height is finished while sculptural work on parts of the basilica continues (no longer flatly 'unfinished', but not fully 'finished' either). Dinner-test payoff = Gaudí capping his tower one metre BELOW the city's hill so man's work stays under God's. Settled wonder; respect for the religious intent is enough without a stance.

name: Granada — the Alhambra's water palace
scope: On a ridge above Granada stands the ALHAMBRA, the palace-city of the Nasrid sultans — the last Muslim kingdom in Western Europe. T1: its name means 'the RED one' (al-Hamra) for the red clay walls that glow at sunset. T2: the Alhambra is a garden built around WATER — channels, pools and fountains everywhere — fed by the ACEQUIA REAL, a canal carrying SNOWMELT down from the Sierra Nevada mountains. T3: in the COURT OF THE LIONS, twelve marble lions ring a fountain and four rills run out toward the four points of the compass — an image of the four rivers of the Islamic paradise garden. T4: the ceilings drip with MUQARNAS — honeycombs of thousands of tiny plaster cells, like a stone stalactite cave, in the Hall of the Two Sisters. T5: the Alhambra was handed over in January 1492 when Granada, the last Muslim-ruled city in Iberia, fell to Ferdinand and Isabella — ending nearly 800 years of al-Andalus and, because the new rulers preserved it, leaving the palace almost intact. (The GENERALIFE summer gardens next door still run their old water staircases.)
source: Grokipedia (Alhambra; Nasrid dynasty) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Alhambra; Court of the Lions; Generalife; Acequia Real; Granada War / 1492); alhambradegranada.org (Court of the Lions, Nasrid palaces).
framing_note: PLACE = the Alhambra/Granada; answers are concrete facts about the palace and its water (the red walls, the Sierra-Nevada snowmelt canal, the Court of the Lions, muqarnas, the 1492 handover). vision_mandated TRUE: celebrate al-Andalus / Nasrid hydraulic engineering as a FULL, sophisticated civilization (never 'exotic' or 'primitive'); respect the Islamic garden as sacred design on its own terms (no smug secular gloss); state the 1492 fall as timeless historical/geographic fact, honest and un-editorialized. Accuracy rail: the water is Sierra Nevada SNOWMELT via the Acequia Real; teach 'muqarnas' (the honeycomb vaulting) before testing it. Dinner-test payoff = a whole palace plumbed by mountain snowmelt, its lion fountain flowing to the four paradise rivers.
history_overlap: The 1492 fall-of-Granada rung may overlap a history-bank Reconquista episode; keep the geography answer place-anchored (the Alhambra preserved intact), not the war narrative.

name: Lisbon — the quake that shook the Enlightenment
scope: Portugal's capital on the wide TAGUS estuary, a launch-point of the Age of Discovery — and site of a disaster that shook Europe's mind. T1: on All Saints' Day, 1 November 1755, a massive EARTHQUAKE struck while the churches were full; about 40 minutes later a TSUNAMI surged up the Tagus, and fires finished what the shaking and water began. T2: the quake (estimated around magnitude 8.5) killed tens of thousands and destroyed most of Lisbon in a single morning — one of Europe's deadliest natural disasters. T3: it 'shook the Enlightenment': that so many died AT CHURCH on a holy day forced thinkers like VOLTAIRE (who wove it into Candide) to argue over how a good God could allow it — a founding moment of the 'problem of evil' debate. T4: the king's minister, the MARQUIS OF POMBAL, ran perhaps the first scientific disaster survey — asking every parish how long the shaking lasted and which way it moved — an origin of modern SEISMOLOGY. T5: Pombal rebuilt downtown on a grid using the GAIOLA POMBALINA — a wooden cage hidden inside the masonry walls so a building could flex and survive the next quake — one of the world's first earthquake-resistant designs, reportedly tested by marching troops around mock-ups.
source: Grokipedia (1755 Lisbon earthquake; Marquis of Pombal) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (1755 Lisbon earthquake; Gaiola (construction) / Pombaline architecture); Britannica (Lisbon earthquake of 1755); Hakai Magazine ('The Earthquake That Brought Enlightenment').
framing_note: PLACE = Lisbon; answers are concrete facts of the 1755 event and its rebuild (the All-Saints quake+tsunami+fire, the Enlightenment reckoning, Pombal's survey, the gaiola cage). Accuracy rail: magnitude is ESTIMATED (~8.5; sources range 7.7–9) — do NOT pin an exact number as the answer; keep the answer the tsunami/fire/gaiola, not the magnitude figure. vision_mandated TRUE (lightly): handle the 'why did God allow it' shock with RESPECT (no smug secular dismissal of the faithful who died at Mass), and celebrate the Age-of-Discovery Tagus honestly. Dinner-test payoff = the hidden wooden 'cage' (gaiola) that lets Pombaline buildings flex through earthquakes.
history_overlap: The Enlightenment / Voltaire response may overlap philosophy or history banks; keep the geography answer the earth-event and the rebuilt place, not the philosophy itself.

name: Amsterdam — the city on piles below the sea
scope: The Dutch capital, a Golden-Age trading city literally built on water and wood, much of it BELOW sea level. T1: Amsterdam is a city of CANALS — its 17th-century 'canal ring' (grachtengordel) is a set of concentric waterways dug in a half-moon around the old town (a UNESCO World Heritage site). T2: the ground is soft peat and clay, so nearly every old building stands on WOODEN PILES driven down to firm sand — the Royal Palace on Dam Square alone rests on 13,659 of them. T3: the very name says how it began — 'Amstel-dam', a DAM built across the little River Amstel around 1270 to hold back the tides. T4: the wider Netherlands lives behind DIKES and pumps land dry into POLDERS; large areas — and parts of Amsterdam — sit BELOW sea level, kept dry only by constant pumping (once by windmills). T5: because the wooden piles must stay underwater or they rot, dropping groundwater lets them decay — and centuries of soft ground leave Amsterdam's narrow gabled canal houses leaning and tilting at odd angles.
source: Grokipedia (Amsterdam; Royal Palace of Amsterdam) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Amsterdam; Canals of Amsterdam / grachtengordel UNESCO; Royal Palace of Amsterdam — 13,659 piles; polder; Dutch flood defences).
framing_note: PLACE = Amsterdam; answers are concrete facts about the water-city (the canal ring, wooden piles, the Amstel dam, polders below sea level, the leaning houses). Invert the wonder: 'the Royal Palace stands on 13,659 of WHAT?' → wooden piles. Accuracy rail: it's the WOODEN PILES driven to firm sand that hold the city (not solid ground); 'below sea level' is true for parts of the city and much of the country, kept dry by pumping. Dinner-test payoff = a stone palace balanced on 13,659 tree-trunks sunk in the mud. Lane border: the PLACE and its land-reclamation engineering, not Dutch trade-empire history.

name: Bruges — the port that froze in time
scope: A medieval Flemish trading city in Belgium, laced with canals — 'the Venice of the North.' T2: its landmark is the BELFRY (Belfort), an 83 m brick tower whose top holds a CARILLON — 47 tuned bells (about 27 tonnes) played from a keyboard, ringing out over the market square. T3: Bruges was one of medieval Europe's richest ports until its lifeline, the ZWIN sea-channel, silted up in the 1400s — cutting the city off from the North Sea and shifting trade to Antwerp. T4: that collapse is exactly why Bruges is so beautiful today: too poor to rebuild, the city was 'frozen in time', preserving its medieval streets and stepped-gable houses almost whole.
source: Grokipedia (Bruges; Belfry of Bruges) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Belfry of Bruges — 47-bell carillon, 83 m; Bruges; the Zwin); Britannica (Brugge).
framing_note: PLACE = Bruges; answers are concrete facts (the 47-bell carillon belfry, the silted Zwin, the accidental preservation). Accuracy rail: the carillon has 47 bells; the Zwin silted in the 15th century → decline → preservation (the cause-and-effect IS the wonder). Dinner-test payoff = the harbour channel silting shut, which impoverished Bruges and thereby SAVED its perfect medieval face. Lane border: keep to the PLACE, not Flemish cloth-trade economics as its own topic (history).

name: Seville — the inland gate to the Americas
scope: The Andalusian city on the GUADALQUIVIR, an inland river-port that became Spain's gateway to the New World. T2: its bell tower, the GIRALDA, began life as the MINARET of a great Almohad mosque (built 1184–1198); after the Christian conquest a Renaissance belfry was added on top, turning a minaret into a cathedral tower about 96 m tall. T3: beside it rises SEVILLE CATHEDRAL, the LARGEST GOTHIC church in the world, raised on the old mosque's footprint — its builders reportedly vowed to make one 'so beautiful that those who see it will think we were mad'. T4: inside, four crowned bearers hold the TOMB of CHRISTOPHER COLUMBUS aloft (DNA testing in 2024 confirmed his remains truly rest here). T5: for over two centuries Seville held Spain's MONOPOLY on trade with the New World — its CASA DE CONTRATACIÓN (House of Trade, from 1503) meant EVERY ship to and from the Americas had to dock in this river city 90 km from the open sea.
source: Grokipedia (Casa de Contratación — seen directly in results) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Giralda; Seville Cathedral; Tomb of Christopher Columbus; Casa de Contratación; History of Seville); archaeologymag.com / 2024 DNA confirmation of Columbus's Seville remains.
framing_note: PLACE = Seville; answers are concrete facts (the minaret-turned-belltower Giralda, the largest Gothic cathedral, Columbus's tomb, the New-World trade monopoly on the Guadalquivir). vision_mandated TRUE: celebrate the Age of Discovery honestly AND handle the Giralda's Almohad origin with respect — a minaret RE-USED, not erased; name both civilizations plainly. Accuracy rail: the Giralda's lower shaft is the original 12th-c. Almohad minaret with a 16th-c. belfry added on top; 'largest GOTHIC church' (St Peter's is bigger but not Gothic). Dinner-test payoff = a river city 90 km inland that every treasure ship from the Americas HAD to sail to.
history_overlap: The Columbus / New-World-trade-monopoly rung may overlap a history-bank Age-of-Discovery episode; keep the answer place-anchored (the inland river-port, the Giralda), not the voyages themselves.

name: Pisa — the tower that sank as it rose
scope: In the Tuscan city of PISA, the cathedral's free-standing bell tower became the world's most famous mistake. T2: the LEANING TOWER began sinking almost as soon as building started in 1173 — because the soft ground on one side (clay, sand and shells) squashed down more than the other, tilting the whole tower. T3: builders pressed on for ~200 years, even curving the upper floors to try to correct the lean, which is why the tower is subtly BANANA-shaped. T4: by the 1990s it leaned a dangerous 5.5° and was edging toward collapse; engineers saved it by scooping soil out from under the HIGH side, easing it back to about 4° — stable, they say, for another 200 years.
source: Grokipedia (Leaning Tower of Pisa) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Leaning Tower of Pisa); Britannica (Leaning Tower of Pisa — construction 1173, soft subsoil, ~3.97° after stabilization); ICE (soil-extraction stabilisation).
framing_note: PLACE = Pisa; answers are concrete facts about the tower's soft-soil tilt (the sinking foundation, the banana curve, the soil-extraction rescue). Invert the wonder: 'why did it start to lean before it was even finished?' → the soft clay/sand ground compressed unevenly. Accuracy rail: the lean is a FOUNDATION/soil problem (not a design choice); engineers removed soil from the HIGH side to reduce the tilt. Dinner-test payoff = fixing a leaning tower by digging dirt out from underneath the TALL side, not the low one. Lane border: keep to the PLACE and its geology, not Galileo's physics experiments (science bank — a one-line legend mention at most).
